overview:
Micchāmi Dukkaḍaṃ (Prakrit: मिच्छामि दुक्कडं) is a foundational expression of forgiveness in Jain lay practice, especially associated with the conclusion of Paryuṣaṇa (Śvetāmbara) and Daśalakṣaṇa (Digambara). The phrase is commonly translated as “May my faults be forgiven” or “I ask forgiveness for any harm I may have caused.” It functions as an ethical reset grounded in ahiṃsā, aparigraha, and the Jain theory of karma, where intentional and unintentional harm create karmic bondage. 

Historically, the phrase emerges from Ardhamāgadhī and Śaurasenī Prakrit usages in canonical and commentarial literature describing kṣamā (forbearance) and kṣamāpanā (asking forgiveness). While the exact phrase “micchāmi dukkaḍaṃ” does not appear verbatim in the earliest āgamas, its linguistic components and doctrinal meaning are directly rooted in canonical teachings on repentance (ālochanā), confession (pratikramaṇa), and the cultivation of universal friendship (maitrī). 

In contemporary practice, Jains use Micchāmi Dukkaḍaṃ to acknowledge that harm may occur through speech, action, or thought. The phrase is addressed to all living beings, not only to specific individuals, reflecting the Jain view that ethical responsibility is universal and continuous. Communities across Śvetāmbara Mūrti-pūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, Terāpanth, and Digambara traditions affirm the phrase, though liturgical contexts differ. 

Scholars note that Micchāmi Dukkaḍaṃ is not merely a social courtesy but a ritualized ethical discipline tied to karmic purification. Traditional commentaries emphasize that forgiveness must be sincere, accompanied by introspection, and grounded in the vows appropriate to one’s stage of life (guṇasthāna).

primary_sources.title: Āvaśyaka Niryukti
primary_sources.author: Bhadrabāhu (traditionally attributed)
primary_sources.notes: While the exact phrase ‘micchāmi dukkaḍaṃ’ is not present, the Niryukti repeatedly frames kṣamā as essential to pratikramaṇa. The doctrinal basis for asking forgiveness is derived from these passages.

primary_sources.title: Dasaveyāliya Sutta (Daśavaikālika)
primary_sources.author: Attributed to Śivārya
primary_sources.original_text: मित्ति भणइ जोगो, अमित्ति भणइ पावं
primary_sources.transliteration: mitti bhaṇai jogo, amitti bhaṇai pāvaṃ
primary_sources.translation: “Friendship is the path of discipline; enmity is the path of sin.”
primary_sources.notes: This passage is frequently cited in traditional commentaries to explain why Micchāmi Dukkaḍaṃ is addressed universally to all beings.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.12
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.notes: Commentaries (Kūṇḍakunda, Pūjyapāda, Siddhasena) link pratikramaṇa with confession and forgiveness, forming the doctrinal basis for Micchāmi Dukkaḍaṃ.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 29
primary_sources.author: Unknown (Śvetāmbara canon)
primary_sources.notes: Used in monastic instruction; later lay commentaries apply this to the ethic of mutual forgiveness during Paryuṣaṇa.

misconceptions.myth: Micchāmi Dukkaḍaṃ is only a polite social greeting exchanged during festivals.
misconceptions.reality: Traditional sources frame it as a karmic and ethical practice rooted in pratikramaṇa. It is a ritualized act of repentance and universal forgiveness, not merely a cultural courtesy.

misconceptions.myth: The phrase appears verbatim in early Jain āgamas.
misconceptions.reality: The exact wording does not occur in the earliest canonical texts. However, its linguistic components and doctrinal meaning are directly derived from canonical teachings on kṣamā, ālochanā, and pratikramaṇa.

misconceptions.myth: Micchāmi Dukkaḍaṃ is only used by Śvetāmbara Jains.
misconceptions.reality: Digambara communities also use the phrase or close variants, especially during Daśalakṣaṇa. The underlying ethic of forgiveness is shared across Jain traditions.
